text: Lesson 6 gave you where, project, and take — operators that work one row at a time. This lesson introduces summarize, the operator that collapses many rows into one row per group, paired with three aggregation functions: count, dcount, and avg.

Start with the last seven days of SigninLogs, keep only failed sign-ins, then summarize count of rows by UserPrincipalName — that collapses every row down to one row per distinct user, with FailedSignIns holding how many failures that user had. sort by FailedSignIns desc puts the worst offenders first. Count failures, group by user, sort descending: one of the most common hunting queries written against Sentinel, because an unusually high count is a classic password-spray signal.

count counts rows; dcount counts distinct values instead. This groups by user again, but counts how many different IP addresses each user signed in from over the week. A legitimate user might sign in from two or three IPs — home, office, phone. A user suddenly showing forty distinct IPs is a strong signal worth investigating.

avg works the same summarize-by shape, just with a numeric mean instead of a count. Here the Perf table, performance counters from any connected machine, is filtered to CPU utilization samples, then averaged per Computer — one average CPU reading per machine, the same grouping pattern as the sign-in examples, just a different function over a different column.

Three aggregation functions, one operator. count answers how many rows. dcount answers how many distinct values. avg answers what's the mean. All three plug into the exact same summarize-by shape, which is why learning that shape once pays off across every query you'll write from here on.

Next up: joining tables and time windows. You'll combine SigninLogs with a threat intelligence table using join, filtered to the last 24 hours with ago — correlating a sign-in with exactly why its IP address is considered malicious, a real pattern straight out of Sentinel hunting queries.
